answer.summary: Orosz recommends creating external deadlines and a repeatable schedule, using a short distraction-free timer to get started, and protecting focus time. He also cautions that feeling unproductive may mean you need a break, not simply more pressure.

sections.heading: Build structure with deadlines
sections.content: Orosz says deadlines help him follow through because pressure makes him focus. For his newsletter, he added a second issue to create a steady cadence: he starts the Thursday issue on Wednesday, finishes it Thursday, and starts the next Tuesday issue on Friday. He connects that pressure both to deadlines and to knowing that paying readers expect his work. He also values an open calendar and few meetings so he has time to focus.

sections.heading: Make starting easier
sections.content: When he struggles to begin, Orosz sets a 20-minute timer and commits to doing only the task, with no distractions. He blocks sites such as LinkedIn, Twitter, and Facebook using a simple script. He says he may resist for the first few minutes, but after about five minutes he often gets absorbed in the work. He found the Pomodoro method useful for a few months, though he says tools and methods can become less effective with time.

sections.heading: Add external structure, but notice when you need rest
sections.content: Orosz misses the schedule and built-in pressure of corporate work; independent workers might take a practical lesson from his approach of creating their own regular commitments. He uses a shared workspace to get some social contact. At the same time, he says he has not figured out whether guilt about not working harder is a sign to push through or a signal from his mind or body that he needs a break.

judgment.explanation: The answer is grounded in the cited material and gives useful advice about deadlines, scheduling, and getting started. It mentions that paying readers expect his work, but it does not clearly convey the key advice to tell others when to expect the work, making that external promise a source of accountability and structure.
